title: Filtering Rows with WHERE and Logical Operators
summary: Learn to filter query results with WHERE, combine conditions using AND, OR, and NOT, control evaluation order with parentheses, and test for missing values with IS NULL.

steps.title: Filtering rows with WHERE
steps.lede: Ask a question of your data by keeping only the rows where a condition is true.

blocks.text: SELECT * FROM orders returns every order in the QuickCart database. To answer a real question — which orders took longer than 40 minutes to deliver? — you need to narrow the result to just the matching rows. WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for every row. A row is kept only if the condition is true; rows where it is false are discarded.

The comparison operators <, >, <=, >=, =, and <> compare two values of the same or a compatible type and produce a boolean result. = tests for equal; <> tests for not equal (!= is an alias for <>). WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only orders from customer 2; WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20 keeps orders whose delivery time is not 20 minutes.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40

after.caption: After WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 — only rows where the condition is true

blocks.change_summary: WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps only the five orders whose delivery time exceeds 40 minutes; the other rows are discarded.

steps.title: Pick the right comparison operator
steps.lede: Choose the operator that matches the filter requirement.

public.prompt:
You need to keep only orders where the delivery time is strictly less than 20 minutes. Which comparison operator belongs in the WHERE clause?

WHERE delivery_time_minutes ___ 20

opt_lt.message: Correct. < tests strict less-than, so delivery_time_minutes < 20 keeps only rows where the time is below 20 minutes.

opt_lte.message: Close, but <= includes the boundary: a row with exactly 20 minutes would also be kept. The requirement says strictly less than 20.

opt_eq.message: = tests for equality, not less-than. WHERE delivery_time_minutes = 20 would keep only orders with exactly 20 minutes.

opt_ne.message: <> tests for not-equal. WHERE delivery_time_minutes <> 20 would keep every order except those with exactly 20 minutes — not the same as less than 20.

correct.message: Right. < is the strict less-than operator. The six comparison operators are <, >, <=, >=, =, and <> — each tests a different relationship between two values.

incorrect.message: Think about what 'strictly less than' means. The six operators are <, >, <=, >=, =, and <>. Which one tests that the left side is below the right side without including the boundary?

hints: The requirement says 'strictly less than' — that means the boundary value (20) should not be included.
There are two operators that involve less-than: one includes the boundary and one does not.

steps.title: Write a WHERE clause for a requirement
steps.lede: Select the WHERE clause that correctly expresses the stated filter.

public.prompt: A manager asks: 'Show me all orders placed by customer 3.' Which WHERE clause correctly expresses this requirement?

opt_correct.message: Correct. WHERE customer_id = 3 evaluates to true for every row where customer_id equals 3, and those rows are kept.

opt_ne.message: <> tests for not-equal. WHERE customer_id <> 3 would keep every order except those from customer 3 — the opposite of what was asked.

opt_gt.message: > tests greater-than. WHERE customer_id > 3 would keep orders from customers with an id above 3, not specifically customer 3.

opt_no_where.message: The filter condition belongs in a WHERE clause, not in the SELECT list. SELECT customer_id = 3 would return a boolean column, not filter rows.

correct.message: Right. WHERE evaluates the condition for each row and keeps only those where it is true. = tests for equality, so WHERE customer_id = 3 keeps exactly the rows from customer 3.

incorrect.message: The WHERE clause takes a condition that is evaluated for each row. Think about which operator tests whether two values are equal.

hints: The requirement is 'orders placed by customer 3' — you need to test whether customer_id equals a specific value.
The = operator tests for equality. Which option uses = to compare customer_id to 3?

steps.title: Write a WHERE filter in SQL
steps.lede: Query the QuickCart orders table to return only the orders that exceed a delivery threshold.

public.prompt:
The QuickCart operations team wants to investigate slow deliveries. Write a query that returns the `order_id` and `delivery_time_minutes` for every order where `delivery_time_minutes` is greater than 30.

Your result must have exactly two columns: `order_id` and `delivery_time_minutes`.

files.content:
-- Return order_id and delivery_time_minutes
-- for orders where delivery_time_minutes is greater than 30.
-- Write your SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... query below.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content: SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 30

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return exactly the orders where delivery_time_minutes > 30. Check your WHERE condition and make sure you select only order_id and delivery_time_minutes.

correct.message: Well done. Your WHERE clause evaluated the condition for each row and kept only those where delivery_time_minutes is above 30.

incorrect.message: Check your WHERE clause. The condition should test whether delivery_time_minutes is greater than 30, and your SELECT should return only order_id and delivery_time_minutes.

hints: The structure is: SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE ...
The > operator tests strict greater-than. What condition keeps rows where delivery_time_minutes is above 30?

steps.title: Combining conditions with AND, OR, and NOT
steps.lede: Join multiple filter conditions to express precise requirements.

blocks.text: A WHERE clause often needs more than one condition at once — for example, orders from customer 1 that also took longer than 30 minutes. AND, OR, and NOT let you combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true; NOT reverses a true or false value.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2

left.caption: Without parentheses: AND binds first, then OR

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2)

right.caption: With parentheses: OR is evaluated first inside the group

blocks.takeaway: The same three conditions produce different result sets depending on where the parentheses go — AND always binds before OR unless you override it.

steps.title: Evaluation order and parentheses
steps.lede: NOT binds tightest, then AND, then OR — use parentheses to override.

blocks.text: Without parentheses, NOT is evaluated before AND, and AND before OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2, keeping any order from customer 2 regardless of delivery time.

Parentheses force a different evaluation order. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR first; because customer_id = 1 already rules out customer_id = 2, this version keeps only customer 1 orders that took longer than 30 minutes. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order not from customer 1.

steps.title: Predict the result of unparenthesized conditions
steps.lede: Trace the default evaluation order to predict which rows a query returns.

public.prompt:
Consider this WHERE clause with no parentheses:

WHERE region = 'south' AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR region = 'north'

Which rows does SQL keep?

options.text: Orders from the south region with delivery > 30 minutes, plus all orders from the north region (regardless of delivery time).
Orders that are from the south region AND have delivery > 30 minutes AND are from the north region.
Orders from the south region with delivery > 30 minutes, but only if they are also from the north region.
Only orders from the south region with delivery > 30 minutes — the OR clause is ignored without parentheses.

opt_correct.message: Correct. Without parentheses, AND binds before OR. The expression is read as (region = 'south' AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR region = 'north', so all north-region orders are included regardless of delivery time.

opt_all_and.message: No row can be in both 'south' and 'north' at the same time, so this would return nothing. AND and OR are separate operators — OR does not become AND without parentheses.

opt_or_first.message: This describes an AND of all three conditions, not an OR. Without parentheses, AND binds before OR, so the OR is evaluated last — it does not disappear.

opt_south_only.message: The OR clause is not ignored — it is evaluated last. Without parentheses, AND binds first: (region = 'south' AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR region = 'north'. The OR adds all north-region orders.

correct.message: Right. Without parentheses, AND is evaluated before OR. The clause becomes (region = 'south' AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR region = 'north', which includes every north-region order.

incorrect.message: Remember the default precedence: NOT first, then AND, then OR. Apply AND to the two conditions on either side of it first, then apply OR to the result.

hints: Without parentheses, AND binds before OR — apply AND to its two neighbours first.
After applying AND, you have two groups joined by OR. OR keeps a row if either group is true.

steps.title: Use parentheses to force evaluation order
steps.lede: Choose the version of the WHERE clause that uses parentheses to match the stated requirement.

public.prompt:
A manager asks: 'Show me orders from customer 1 that took more than 30 minutes, OR any order from customer 2 — regardless of delivery time.'

Which WHERE clause correctly expresses this requirement, using explicit parentheses?

options.text: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2

opt_correct.message: Correct. The parentheses group the AND condition first, then OR adds all customer-2 orders. This matches the requirement exactly.

opt_wrong_parens.message: This groups the OR inside the AND: customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2). Because customer_id = 1 already rules out customer_id = 2, the OR has no effect — only customer 1's slow orders are returned, and no customer-2 orders.

opt_no_parens.message: Without parentheses, AND binds before OR, so this is read as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2 — which happens to be the same as the correct answer. But the requirement is to use parentheses to make the grouping explicit and unambiguous.

opt_left_right.message: This uses region columns, not customer_id or delivery_time_minutes, so it does not match the requirement about customers 1 and 2 at all.

correct.message: Right. Parentheses around the AND group make the intent explicit: first apply the AND, then OR adds the customer-2 orders.

incorrect.message: Read the requirement carefully: customer 1 with slow delivery, OR customer 2 regardless of delivery time. Think about which part should be grouped with AND and where the OR should apply.

hints: The requirement has two parts joined by OR: (customer 1 slow orders) OR (any customer 2 order). Which option groups those two parts correctly?
Parentheses force the AND to be evaluated first. The OR then adds the second group.

Use parentheses so the grouping matches the requirement exactly. Your result must have exactly three columns: `order_id`, `customer_id`, `delivery_time_minutes`.

tests.message_on_fail: Your query should return orders from customer 1 with delivery > 30 minutes, plus all north-region orders. Check your parentheses and conditions.

steps.title: Testing for missing values with IS NULL
steps.lede: Missing values are unknown — use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL, never = NULL.

blocks.text: Some orders in the QuickCart database have no recorded delivery time — the value is missing, not zero. SQL represents a missing value with NULL. NULL means unknown: it is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so testing for NULL with an ordinary comparison operator does not work.

To test whether a value is or is not null, use the predicates IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL finds the orders with a missing delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL finds the rest.

Writing WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL does not test for null. NULL is not considered 'equal to' NULL, so that comparison never evaluates to true, and the query silently returns zero rows instead of the missing-time orders you meant to find.

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL

before.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL — returns no rows (= NULL never evaluates to true)

result_of.sql: SELECT order_id, customer_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL

after.caption: WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL — returns the two orders with a missing delivery time

blocks.change_summary: Replacing = NULL with IS NULL returns the rows with a missing delivery time; = NULL silently returns nothing because NULL is not considered equal to NULL.

steps.title: Testing for missing values (video)
steps.lede: See IS NULL and IS NOT NULL in action on a live query.

segments.label: Testing for missing values with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL
segments.summary: Explains that IS NULL gives true when a value is missing and IS NOT NULL gives the opposite, written as a value or expression followed by the keywords. Slide examples on a shipping address and a price show these checks producing true or false flags. A live query then finds a row whose score is missing by using IS NULL rather than an equals sign, and a second query keeps only rows where the score is present with IS NOT NULL.

bridge.before: Watch for the rule that missing values are found with IS NULL rather than an equals sign. The clip opens directly on the definition.
bridge.after: The clip says to use IS NULL instead of equals but not why. The text above explains that a missing value is unknown, so an equals test never comes out true.

steps.title: Why does = NULL never match?
steps.lede: Explain why a query with = NULL returns no rows.

public.prompt:
A developer writes:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes = NULL

The query runs without error but returns zero rows, even though two orders have a missing delivery time. Why?

options.text: NULL represents an unknown value. The = operator never evaluates to true when comparing to NULL, so no rows are kept.
The query has a syntax error — NULL cannot appear on the right side of =.
NULL is treated as zero, and no order has delivery_time_minutes = 0.
The rows with missing delivery times are excluded from the table automatically, so there is nothing to match.

opt_correct.message: Correct. NULL means unknown. It is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so = NULL never evaluates to true — not even for rows where the value is actually missing.

opt_syntax.message: The query is syntactically valid and runs without error. The problem is not syntax — it is that = NULL never evaluates to true, so no rows pass the filter.

opt_zero.message: NULL is not zero. NULL means the value is unknown or absent. Treating it as zero is a common misconception; SQL stores NULL separately from any numeric value.

opt_missing.message: Rows with NULL values are stored in the table normally — they are not removed. The problem is that = NULL never evaluates to true, so those rows are filtered out by the WHERE clause.

correct.message: Right. NULL is unknown, and an unknown value is not considered equal to anything — including another unknown. Use IS NULL to find rows where a value is missing.

incorrect.message: Think about what NULL means in SQL. It is not zero, not an empty string, and not a syntax error. What does NULL represent, and how does that affect the = operator?

hints: NULL means the value is unknown or absent — not zero, not empty.
If a value is unknown, can you say it is equal to NULL? What does SQL do when it cannot determine whether a condition is true?

steps.title: Write IS NULL and IS NOT NULL filters
steps.lede: Query the orders table to find rows with a missing delivery time, then rows where it is present.

public.prompt:
Write **two queries** in the file below, in this order:

1. A query that returns `order_id` and `delivery_time_minutes` for every order where `delivery_time_minutes` **IS NULL** (the delivery time is missing).

2. A query that returns `order_id` and `delivery_time_minutes` for every order where `delivery_time_minutes` **IS NOT NULL** (the delivery time is present).

Do not use `= NULL` in either query. Each query must return exactly two columns: `order_id` and `delivery_time_minutes`.

files.content:
-- Query 1: orders where delivery_time_minutes IS NULL
-- Write your first SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... query here.


-- Query 2: orders where delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL
-- Write your second SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... query here.

blocked_syntax: ON with AND across several columns
subquery in FROM with an alias

solution_files.content:
SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL;

SELECT order_id, delivery_time_minutes FROM orders WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL;

tests.message_on_fail: Your second query should return exactly the 11 orders where delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL. Use IS NOT NULL.

correct.message: Well done. IS NOT NULL finds the rows with a present delivery time, and IS NULL finds the rest. Together they cover the whole table.

incorrect.message: Check both queries. Use IS NULL for the first query and IS NOT NULL for the second. Do not use = NULL — it never matches.

hints: The first query uses WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL. The second uses WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL.
Make sure you write two separate SELECT statements, one for each condition.

steps.title: Recap: Filtering Rows
steps.lede: Three tools for precise row selection: WHERE, logical operators, and IS NULL.

blocks.text: WHERE evaluates a condition for every row and keeps only those where it is true. Comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=, =, <>) produce the boolean result. AND, OR, and NOT combine conditions; AND binds before OR unless you add parentheses. NULL means unknown — use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for missing values; = NULL never matches.

blocks.title: Next: Sorting Results with ORDER BY
blocks.text: WHERE decides which rows come back, but not what order they appear in. Next you will use ORDER BY to sort results from slowest to fastest delivery — or any other direction you need.

remediation_steps.title: Comparison operators: which one to use
remediation_steps.lede: Each comparison operator tests a different relationship between two values.

blocks.text: The six comparison operators are <, >, <=, >=, =, and <>. = tests whether two values are equal; <> (or !=) tests whether they are not equal. < and > test strict less-than and greater-than; <= and >= include the boundary value. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 keeps rows where the time is strictly above 40; WHERE delivery_time_minutes >= 40 would also keep a row with exactly 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: How WHERE evaluates each row
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE tests the condition against every row and keeps only those where it is true.

blocks.text: WHERE takes a search condition and evaluates it for each row in the table. A row is kept only if the condition evaluates to true; rows where it is false are discarded. SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 keeps only the rows where customer_id equals 2 and discards every other row.

remediation_steps.title: Which rows does WHERE keep?
remediation_steps.lede: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is true for that row.

blocks.text: Think of WHERE as a row-by-row question: for each row, is this condition true? If yes, the row appears in the result. If no, it is discarded. WHERE delivery_time_minutes > 40 asks that question for every order in the QuickCart table and returns only the orders where the delivery time is above 40 minutes.

remediation_steps.title: Default evaluation order: NOT, then AND, then OR
remediation_steps.lede: Without parentheses, AND always binds before OR — which can change the rows you get.

blocks.text: When you write multiple conditions without parentheses, SQL evaluates NOT first, then AND, then OR. WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2 is treated as (customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30) OR customer_id = 2. That keeps every order from customer 2, regardless of delivery time — which may not be what you intended.

remediation_steps.title: Using parentheses to control AND/OR grouping
remediation_steps.lede: Parentheses override the default precedence so the OR is evaluated where you need it.

blocks.text: AND, OR, and NOT combine boolean conditions. AND is true only when both sides are true; OR is true when at least one side is true. By default AND binds before OR. Adding parentheses forces the OR to be evaluated first: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (delivery_time_minutes > 30 OR customer_id = 2) evaluates the OR group first, then applies the AND — giving a different result set.

remediation_steps.title: AND, OR, and NOT: combining conditions
remediation_steps.lede: Use AND to require both conditions, OR to accept either, and NOT to exclude.

blocks.text: AND requires both conditions to be true: WHERE customer_id = 1 AND delivery_time_minutes > 30 keeps only customer 1's slow orders. OR accepts either: WHERE customer_id = 1 OR customer_id = 2 keeps orders from either customer. NOT reverses a condition: WHERE NOT (customer_id = 1) keeps every order that is not from customer 1.

remediation_steps.title: Why = NULL never matches
remediation_steps.lede: NULL means unknown — and an unknown value is not considered equal to anything, including another unknown.

blocks.text: NULL represents an unknown value. It is not known whether two unknown values are equal, so the comparison delivery_time_minutes = NULL never evaluates to true — not even when the value is actually missing. The query runs without error but silently returns zero rows, which is not what you want when looking for missing delivery times.

remediation_steps.title: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL: the right predicates
remediation_steps.lede: Use IS NULL to find missing values and IS NOT NULL to find present ones.

blocks.text: To test whether a value is missing, use IS NULL. To test whether a value is present, use IS NOT NULL. WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NULL returns the orders with no recorded delivery time; WHERE delivery_time_minutes IS NOT NULL returns the orders that do have one. Together these two predicates cover the whole table.
